content: The World Health Organization (WHO) developed a comprehensive document in 2015 to consolidate all recommendations and technical guidance on HIV testing services (HTS) into a single, user-friendly resource. This document includes a series of web annexes that provide in-depth information, including case examples of HTS approaches. These case examples aim to supplement published literature and highlight innovative strategies for delivering HIV testing services, particularly to key populations disproportionately affected by HIV, such as men who have sex with men (MSM), sex workers, people who inject drugs (PWID), transgender individuals, and people in prisons or other closed settings. These populations experience HIV prevalence rates 10 to 50 times higher than the general population, and they account for approximately 40% of all new adult HIV infections annually. Despite the global expansion of HIV testing and treatment services, key populations remain underserved due to stigma, discrimination, and criminalization of their behaviors. Efforts to increase access to HTS for these groups have often been small-scale, with limited coverage and insufficient evidence in resource-limited settings. To address these gaps, the WHO collected case examples from the field to inspire new strategies for increasing HIV testing uptake, repeat testing for high-risk populations, and linkage to care and treatment. The case examples presented in the annex cover a range of topics, including unique service delivery approaches, critical enablers, the use of lay providers, promotional strategies, and methods to enhance linkage to care. These examples were collected using a structured methodology adapted from the WHO Consolidated Guidelines on HIV diagnosis, prevention, care, and treatment for key populations. Contributors were identified through a review of recent WHO guidelines, outreach to regional offices, UN partners, civil society networks, and other organizations providing HIV services. Participation was voluntary, and organizations could choose to remain anonymous in public documents. A total of 45 case examples were submitted, with 43 meeting the initial criteria for consideration. These examples showcased interventions supported by governments, UN agencies, international and national NGOs, and community-based organizations. The programs offered a variety of services, including HIV testing, counseling, STI screening and treatment, antiretroviral therapy, and advocacy and social support. After further review and editing, 40 case examples were included for online ranking by the WHO Steering Group and Guidelines Development Group. Ultimately, 18 case examples were fully integrated into the Consolidated Guidelines on HTS, while others were highlighted for their high quality and unique contributions. The case examples provide detailed descriptions of program activities, successes, and challenges. For instance, the Excellence and Friends Management Care Centre (EFMC) in Nigeria implemented an integrated HIV prevention program targeting people in prisons and sex workers. In prisons, EFMC engaged with prison authorities to provide education on the importance of knowing one’s HIV status and offered free HTS. Between May and September 2013, over 800 prisoners were tested, with 34 individuals diagnosed as HIV-positive and successfully linked to care and treatment. Similarly, EFMC worked with sex workers in brothels, using community engagement and behavior change communication to create demand for HTS. From 2013 to 2014, 1,466 sex workers were tested, with 189 diagnosed as HIV-positive and 145 linked to care and treatment. In Mozambique, Jhpiego supported a home-based HTS program using lay counselors from local community and faith-based groups. The program also referred HIV-negative men to voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) services, contributing to the circumcision of over 322,000 men by 2015. In Kenya, LVCT Health developed a program to address the sexual and reproductive health needs of MSM and sex workers, who often face barriers to accessing health services due to stigma and criminalization. Between 2011 and 2014, over 8,000 individuals accessed integrated HIV prevention, treatment, and care services, with high rates of treatment adherence and viral suppression among those diagnosed as HIV-positive. The MOSAIC Men’s Health Initiative in South Africa, launched by the International Center for AIDS Care and Treatment Programs (ICAP) in 2012, aimed to increase access to HIV prevention services for MSM. The program provided mobile HTS, STI and TB screening, substance abuse and mental health referrals, and linkage to care for HIV-positive individuals. By 2015, the program had reached nearly 14,000 MSM with HIV prevention services and trained over 2,000 healthcare workers. These case examples demonstrate the importance of innovative, community-driven approaches to HIV testing and care. They highlight the need for tailored interventions to address the unique challenges faced by key populations and emphasize the role of collaboration between governments, civil society, and community organizations in achieving effective and sustainable HIV prevention and treatment outcomes.
